Top 5 AI customer-service agents, by pricing model

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 22 October 2026 · 8-minute read · Revenue

Customer service is the one place outcome pricing has taken hold, because a resolved ticket can be counted. That makes the definition of "resolved" the most important line in the contract. Fin and Zendesk now publish exactly what counts as a billable event; Salesforce publishes three pricing models for Agentforce; Sierra and Decagon still ask you to call sales. Fin ranks first for a published $0.99 price and the largest customer base, followed by Zendesk, Sierra, Agentforce and Decagon.

Outcome-based pricing means paying per counted result rather than per seat or per call. Our explainer on outcome-based pricing for AI sets out how it works, and lowob's piece Seats, usage or outcomes argues when each model fits. Customer service is where the model works best because the unit is visible: a conversation either ended with the customer's problem solved or it did not. Zendesk's 2024 announcement put it simply: customers "will only incur costs for issues that are resolved autonomously by AI". Sierra's co-founder Bret Taylor described the idea in 2025 as "let's pay for a job well done". The hard part is the word "resolved".

How we ranked

CriterionWeightWhy it matters
Pricing transparency30%A published unit price is the only way to model cost before a sales call.

The list

1. Fin (formerly Intercom; now owned by Salesforce)

Best for: teams that want a published price and the largest customer base.

Why it ranks first: $0.99 per outcome on a public price list, charged at most once per conversation even if Fin takes several actions. A resolution counts when the customer confirms the answer helped or leaves without asking for more, and "only when Fin provides an actual answer"; a greeting alone does not count. Salesforce agreed on 15 June 2026 to buy Fin for about $3.6 billion, citing more than 30,000 customer companies and examples of AI agents resolving on average 76% of support volume end to end.

Watch out for: "outcome" is now broader than "resolution". A procedure handoff to a human or workflow, a disqualified prospect and a self-serve routing each cost $0.99, and a qualified prospect costs $9.99. Model your volume on the new definition, not last year's. Voice and high-volume pricing go through sales. The acquisition also raises roadmap questions for firms that do not run Salesforce; the June release did not say whether Fin stays available on other help desks.

Pricing: $0.99 per resolution, procedure handoff, disqualification or self-serve routing; $9.99 per qualification, for chat and email (as listed in November 2026).

What would change its rank: product or pricing changes as it is folded into Salesforce.

2. Zendesk AI agents

Best for: teams already on Zendesk.

Why it ranks here: the clearest rule on what is billable. Under resolution tiers introduced on 18 May 2026, every conversation lands in one of three buckets. An assisted escalation, where a human finished the job, is not counted. A contained resolution, where the customer did not ask for more help, is not counted either. Only a verified resolution is billed, and verification is "performed by an LLM that evaluates the text of the conversation". A conversation ends 72 hours after the first email, two hours after the first message by default, or when a call ends.

Watch out for: the verification is still Zendesk's own model marking Zendesk's own work. Ask how often a verified resolution is reopened. Zendesk's help article describes the tiers but not the price; third-party teardowns put it at about $1.50 per automated resolution on a committed annual plan and about $2.00 pay-as-you-go, falling with volume, with a small included allowance per agent.

Pricing: about $1.50 committed and $2.00 pay-as-you-go per verified resolution, per third-party reporting in July 2026; confirm on your quote.

What would change its rank: a published rate card on Zendesk's own pages, or disclosed resolution rates.

3. Sierra

Best for: large consumer brands wanting a fully managed agent.

Why it ranks here: priced on outcomes, with customers billed when the agent resolves a case and nothing when a human has to take over, and the strongest growth story in the category. Sierra told TechCrunch it reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue in late November 2025 and $150 million in early February 2026, and claims more than 40% of the Fortune 50 as customers. On 4 May 2026 it announced a $950 million round led by Tiger Global and GV at a valuation above $15 billion.

Watch out for: no published rates, so every price is negotiated, and every growth figure above is the company's own.

Pricing: outcome-based, through sales.

What would change its rank: a published rate card.

4. Salesforce Agentforce

Best for: Salesforce shops that want agents across sales and service, not service alone.

Why it ranks here: the broadest product, and all its pricing models are published. Customer-facing agents can be bought at $2 per conversation, or on Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 credits, where a standard action costs 20 credits (about $0.10) and a voice action 30. Per-user add-ons for sales, service and field service are $125 a month with unmetered employee use, and Max Edition starts at $550 per user a month with 2.75 million Flex Credits a year included.

Watch out for: complexity. Flex Credits and per-conversation pricing cannot be used in the same org, switching means replacing every conversation SKU, and unused Flex Credits do not roll over. Salesforce notes the prices are for information and may change. With Fin also now under Salesforce, expect the two product lines to converge.

Pricing: $2 per conversation; Flex Credits $500 per 100,000; add-ons from $125 per user a month (as listed in November 2026).

What would change its rank: a simpler buying model.

5. Decagon

Best for: enterprises that want a challenger with room to negotiate.

Why it ranks here: a $250 million Series D at a $4.5 billion valuation announced on 27 January 2026, which Decagon says tripled its valuation in under six months. It says it added more than 100 enterprise customers in its last fiscal year and names Avis Budget Group, Deutsche Telekom, Block, Affirm and Chime among them.

Watch out for: no published rates and no disclosed revenue. Reports have described a choice of per-conversation or a higher per-resolution price on annual contracts, but Decagon's own announcement does not mention pricing, and we could not confirm it.

Pricing: through sales.

What would change its rank: published pricing and independent resolution data.

In an outcome contract, the definition of the outcome is the price. Read it before you read the rate.

Left out, and why

ServiceNow. Strong for internal service desks, which is a different category; this list is about customer-facing agents, and we could not confirm a list price for its AI on its own pages this month.

Three questions for any vendor

  1. Exactly what event triggers a charge, and who verifies it? Fin bills on customer behaviour; Zendesk on its own model's verdict. Both are reasonable; neither is neutral.
  2. Show us last quarter's resolution rate for a customer like us, measured by the customer, not the vendor. Ask for the reopen rate on billed resolutions alongside it.
  3. What happens to the price if our volume doubles, or halves? Committed tiers, minimums and non-rolling credits all change the answer. Our explainer on usage-based pricing for AI covers how to model it.

Whatever you buy, keep a person on anything that commits the firm: refunds above a threshold, contract changes, anything legal. Our piece Nothing sends without a person sets out where that line usually sits.

lowob takeaways

  • Fin ranks first on transparency. $0.99 per outcome, published, but "outcome" now covers handoffs, disqualifications and routings.
  • Zendesk has the clearest billing rule. Only LLM-verified resolutions are billed, since 18 May 2026.
  • Sierra has the growth and no rate card. Outcome pricing, negotiated every time.
  • Agentforce publishes everything and simplifies nothing. Three models, and two cannot be mixed.
Gateway card

Buyer's checklist for an AI customer-service agent

  • The contract defines the billable event in one sentence
  • You know who verifies that the event happened, and can audit a sample
  • Escalations, greetings and reopened tickets are explicitly not billed
  • The reopen rate on billed resolutions is reported monthly
  • The price at double and half your current volume is written into the quote
  • A person approves refunds, credits and contract changes above a set threshold
